OG-18.from:
Solar in New Zealand

NZ receives approximately 1,400–2,000 sunshine hours annually depending on region. A typical 5kW residential solar system in Auckland generates 6,500–7,500 kWh per year — enough to cover most household consumption. With grid-tie, you sell excess back. With batteries, you store it for night and outages.
OG-18.to:
What affects how much solar you get

How much electricity a solar system generates depends on where you live, the direction and tilt of your roof, shading, and the season. With a grid connection, you can sell solar electricity you don't use back to your power company. A battery lets you store solar electricity for the evening. It can also keep essentials running during an outage — but only if the system is designed to provide backup power: solar panels on their own will not.
OG-18.reason: Removes the unsourced sunshine-hours range (1,400–2,000), the Auckland 5 kW generation figure (6,500–7,500 kWh) and 'enough to cover most household consumption'. Corrects 'With batteries, you store it for … outages' (OG-19 rule: backup depends on the system). EECA: sell unused solar 'back to your power company'; 'solar without battery will not provide power during an outage'.

OG-18.from:
Solar in New Zealand

NZ receives approximately 1,400–2,000 sunshine hours annually depending on region. A typical 5kW residential solar system in Auckland generates 6,500–7,500 kWh per year — enough to cover most household consumption. With grid-tie, you sell excess back. With batteries, you store it for night and outages.
OG-18.to:
What affects how much solar you get

How much electricity a solar system generates depends on where you live, the direction and tilt of your roof, shading, and the season. With a grid connection, solar electricity you don't use can be exported to the grid, and your electricity retailer may pay you a feed-in tariff for it. A battery lets you store solar electricity for the evening. It can also keep essentials running during an outage — but only if the system is designed to provide backup power: solar panels on their own will not.
OG-18.reason: As NZ, and 'Solar in New Zealand' was New Zealand-only content in the Australian file. energy.gov.au: exports and the retailer's feed-in tariff; 'Many grid-connected solar systems shut down when there is a power outage.'

OG-18.from: Reality Check
OG-18.to:
Ask your installer for the peak sun hours where you live. Treat this as a first estimate only: real generation also depends on your roof, shading, the season and losses in the system, and installers use design software for your site — ask what assumptions their estimate is based on.

Reality Check
OG-18.reason: Replaces the removed fixed assumption with where to get it. energy.gov.au: installers 'usually use specialist solar quoting software' — 'ask them what assumptions their calculations are based on'.

OG-18.from: A "100% offset" system means you generate enough over 24 hours to cover consumption — but timing matters.
OG-18.to: A system sized to cover all your daily use generates that total over the day — but only while the sun is up, so timing matters.
OG-18.reason: Refers to the '100% offset' row, renamed by the Step 3 proposals. Same teaching (generation vs timing), without the bill-offset framing.

OG-18.from: Batteries (covered in OG-19) solve the timing problem.
OG-18.to: A battery can help with the timing — see the Battery Backup Planner. Solar panels on their own will not power your home during a grid outage: backup depends on the battery, the inverter and how the system is set up.
OG-18.reason: Visible OG-19 code → the resource title. Carries forward the OG-19 backup rule (EECA; energy.gov.au).

OG-18.from:
Typical NZ Pricing (2025)

3kW system: $6,000–$8,500 | 5kW system: $9,000–$13,000 | 8kW system: $14,000–$20,000
Payback period: 7–10 years depending on region, electricity rates, and usage pattern. Add $8,000–$15,000 for battery storage.
OG-18.to:
Comparing quotes

Ask for written quotes that list everything included. Compare the system size, the parts, the estimated yearly generation and savings, and the assumptions each estimate is based on. Prices change, so rely on current quotes rather than published price ranges.
OG-18.reason: Removes unsourced NZ prices (3/5/8 kW systems), 'Payback period: 7–10 years' and '$8,000–$15,000 for battery storage' — NZ-only content in the AU file too. Replacement: EECA checklist ('get a written quote. Make sure it clearly states what's included'); energy.gov.au (ask what assumptions estimates use).
